practices.title: Limit information system access to authorized users, processes acting on behalf of authorized users or devices (including other information systems).
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor starts from the lists: who is allowed in, which service accounts and applications act for those people, and which devices may connect. They compare each list with what the tenant actually holds: enabled user accounts against the authorized-user list, app registrations and service principals against the process list, and enrolled or registered devices against the device inventory. They read the Conditional Access policies to see how access is actually limited, then pick a few names from each tenant list and ask who approved them. Testing usually means trying a sign-in from an account or device that is not on the list and watching it fail.
common_failure_modes: The authorized-user list is missing, or it is an HR roster that does not match the enabled accounts in the tenant.
Service principals and app registrations are left out of the inventory, or several have no owner.
Leavers still have enabled accounts weeks after their last day.
Conditional Access policies exist but run in report-only mode or exclude large groups without a written reason.
Personal or unmanaged devices can sign in because no policy requires a compliant or registered device.

objectives.determination: authorized users are identified
processes acting on behalf of authorized users are identified
devices (and other systems) authorized to connect to the system are identified
system access is limited to authorized users
system access is limited to processes acting on behalf of authorized users
system access is limited to authorized devices (including other systems)

practices.title: Limit information system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants to see, in writing, what each kind of user is allowed to do: which roles exist, which applications and functions each role can use, and what ordinary users cannot do (for example register apps or create groups). They then compare that with the tenant: directory role memberships, group-based access to applications and the default user permissions. They sample a few users, read their actual rights and ask the manager whether those rights match the job. Testing means having an ordinary user try a function their role should not allow.
common_failure_modes: Roles are named but the functions each role may use are never written down.
Default user settings still let anyone register applications, create security groups or invite guests.
Global Administrator is held by more people than the job needs.
Stale, suspended or guest accounts keep rights they no longer need.
Access is granted user by user instead of by role, so nobody can say what a role includes.

objectives.determination: the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute are defined
system access is limited to the defined types of transactions and functions for authorized users

practices.title: Control the flow of CUI in accordance with approved authorizations.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a written flow control policy that says where CUI may go: which networks, people, devices and connected systems are approved sources and destinations, and who authorizes a new flow. They read the data flow diagram and the CUI boundary in the SSP, then read the tenant mechanisms that enforce it: sensitivity labels, data loss prevention rules, sharing limits and membership of CUI sites. They sample a CUI site or Team and check that its members match an approval. Testing means trying to send or share labelled CUI to a destination the policy does not allow and seeing it blocked or flagged.
common_failure_modes: No data flow diagram, or one that leaves out email, file sharing or a connected external system.
A CUI sensitivity label exists but no rule acts on it, so labelled files move freely.
Membership of CUI sites and Teams is never reviewed, and former project members still have access.
Contractor and guest access to CUI locations is granted without a recorded approval.
The policy names flow rules that no tenant setting actually enforces.

objectives.determination: information flow control policies are defined
methods and enforcement mechanisms for controlling the flow of CUI are defined
designated sources and destinations (e.g., networks, individuals, and devices) for CUI within the system and between interconnected systems are identified
authorizations for controlling the flow of CUI are defined
approved authorizations for controlling the flow of CUI are enforced

practices.title: Separate the duties of individuals to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks which duties must not sit with one person (for example requesting and approving privileged access, making and approving changes, running and reviewing audit logs, creating and paying vendors). They want those pairs written down, a named person for each side, and tenant rights that keep the two sides apart. In the tenant they read the PIM policies to see whether activating a privileged role needs someone else's approval, and check that approvers are real people who are not also the requesters. In small organizations they accept compensating review where full separation is impossible, if it is written and done.
common_failure_modes: No list of duties that need separation; the policy only repeats the requirement.
One administrator can request, approve and activate their own privileged role.
PIM approval is configured but the approver is a departed user or the same person as the requester.
In a very small team, no compensating review is written down or carried out.
Audit log review is done by the same people whose actions are being reviewed.

objectives.determination: the duties of individuals requiring separation are defined
responsibilities for duties that require separation are assigned to separate individuals
access privileges that enable individuals to exercise the duties that require separation are granted to separate individuals

practices.title: Employ the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and privileged accounts.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants a list of privileged accounts and of security functions (for example managing roles, Conditional Access, audit settings, Defender and Intune policy), with who may use each one and why. They compare the list with the tenant's role assignments, looking for standing Global Administrator or other high roles that should be eligible through PIM instead, and for people holding more roles than their job needs. They check that the only standing assignments are documented emergency accounts. They ask a few administrators what each of their roles is for.
common_failure_modes: Several people hold permanent Global Administrator rights instead of eligible PIM assignments.
Security functions are never listed, so nobody can say who should manage audit or Conditional Access settings.
Administrators hold broad roles when a narrower built-in role would do the job.
Former administrators keep eligible or active role assignments.
Emergency (break-glass) accounts are not documented, so their standing rights look like ordinary over-privilege.

objectives.determination: privileged accounts are identified
access to privileged accounts is authorized in accordance with the principle of least privilege
security functions are identified
access to security functions is authorized in accordance with the principle of least privilege

practices.title: Use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing non-security functions.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that people who hold administrator rights use a separate, unprivileged account for everyday work like email, web browsing and documents. They read the policy that says so, then compare the tenant's privileged accounts against licences and names: an admin account with a mailbox licence is usually someone's everyday account. They try to match each admin account to the same person's normal account. In interview they ask administrators which account they read email with.
common_failure_modes: Administrators read email and browse the web with the same account that holds their admin roles.
Admin accounts carry productivity licences, so they work as everyday accounts.
Non-security functions are never described, so the rule has nothing to point at.
Third-party apps hold broad delegated permissions that act with administrator reach for everyday tasks.

objectives.determination: nonsecurity functions are identified
users are required to use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing nonsecurity functions

practices.title: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and capture the execution of such functions in audit logs.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants a list of privileged functions and a definition of who counts as a non-privileged user. They check the tenant so that non-privileged accounts cannot reach those functions: no standing admin roles on everyday accounts, privileged roles activated through PIM, default user permissions restricted. They then look for audit records of privileged actions: role activations and directory changes with who, what and when. They pick a few privileged actions from the last month and find them in the logs, and check that emergency accounts are both excluded from blocking policies and tested.
common_failure_modes: Privileged functions are not listed, so it is unclear what non-privileged users must be kept from.
Everyday licensed accounts hold standing privileged roles.
Role activations or admin changes are not in the audit log, or the log is kept too short to cover the sample.
The emergency account is never tested, or a Conditional Access policy would lock it out too.

objectives.determination: privileged functions are defined
non-privileged users are defined
non-privileged users are prevented from executing privileged functions
the execution of privileged functions is captured in audit logs

practices.title: Limit unsuccessful logon attempts.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads how the organization limits failed sign-ins: how many attempts, what happens next (lockout, delay, or a stronger challenge) and for how long. In Entra this is usually smart lockout, so they compare the documented threshold and lockout time with the tenant setting. They also check any other way into the system that has its own logon (local device accounts, VPN, line-of-business apps). Testing means repeated wrong passwords on a test account and confirming the lockout happens as written.
common_failure_modes: No threshold or lockout time is written down, so the setting cannot be judged.
The documented values differ from the tenant's smart lockout settings.
Local device accounts or a separate VPN logon have no failed-attempt limit.
A lockout test was never run, so nobody has seen the control work.

objectives.determination: the means of limiting unsuccessful logon attempts is defined
the defined means of limiting unsuccessful logon attempts is implemented

practices.title:
Provide privacy and security notices consistent with applicable Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) rules.
Assessment Objective:
[a] privacy and security notices required by CUI-specified rules are identified, consistent, 
and associated with the specific CUI category; and
[b] privacy and security notices are displayed.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that the organization has worked out which notices its CUI requires (for example a system use banner, and any notice tied to a specific CUI category such as export-controlled or privacy data) and that the wording fits those categories. They then look for the notice where people actually meet it: at sign-in through Entra Terms of Use, on device logon screens, and on any other system that handles CUI. Testing means signing in and seeing the notice before access is given.
common_failure_modes: A generic banner is used with no check of what the organization's CUI categories require.
The notice appears in the browser sign-in but not on device logon screens or other CUI systems.
Users can dismiss the Terms of Use without viewing it.
Banner wording differs between systems, or still names an old company or policy.

objectives.determination: privacy and security notices required by CUI-specified rules are identified, consistent, and associated with the specific CUI category
privacy and security notices are displayed

practices.title: Use session lock with pattern-hiding displays to prevent access and viewing of data after a period of inactivity.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the defined inactivity period and checks that devices lock after it and hide what was on the screen. In CES tenants this is an Intune device setting, so they read the device configuration or compliance policy for the inactivity timeout and compare it with the documented period. They check that the policy is assigned to all devices that handle CUI. Testing means leaving a device idle and seeing it lock to a screen that shows nothing from the session.
common_failure_modes: No inactivity period is written down.
The Intune setting differs from the documented period, or is assigned to only some device groups.
Devices outside Intune (for example Macs or shared workstations) have no lock setting.
The lock screen still shows notifications or document content.

objectives.determination: the period of inactivity after which the system initiates a session lock is defined
access to the system and viewing of data is prevented by initiating a session lock after the defined period of inactivity
previously visible information is concealed via a pattern-hiding display after the defined period of inactivity

practices.title: Terminate (automatically) user sessions after a defined condition.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the conditions that end a session (for example a maximum session length, a change in user risk, or the account being disabled) and checks that the tenant applies them without anyone acting. In Entra this is mainly a Conditional Access sign-in frequency control, so they compare the documented limit with the policy and its assignment. They also ask how sessions end on applications outside Entra. Testing means waiting past the limit, or disabling a test account, and confirming the session is ended and a new sign-in is asked for.
common_failure_modes: No conditions are written down, only a statement that sessions time out.
Sign-in frequency is not set, set longer than the documented limit, or applied to only some users.
Disabling an account does not end its existing sessions.
Applications that do not sign in through Entra keep sessions open indefinitely.

objectives.determination: conditions requiring a user session to terminate are defined
a user session is automatically terminated after any of the defined conditions occur

practices.title: Monitor and control remote access sessions.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks whether remote access is allowed and, if so, which kinds (for example web sign-in to Microsoft 365 from home, VPN, remote desktop, vendor support tools). They read how each kind is controlled, such as Conditional Access with named locations and device rules, and how it is watched, such as sign-in logs that record where each session came from. They sample sign-ins from outside the office and check each was allowed by a rule and is visible in the logs. They also ask who reviews remote sign-ins and how often.
common_failure_modes: The kinds of remote access in use are not listed, so a vendor support tool or remote desktop is missed.
Named locations are out of date and still trust old office ranges.
Admin portals can be reached from any address.
Sign-in logs are collected but nobody reviews them.

objectives.determination: remote access sessions are permitted
the types of permitted remote access are identified
remote access sessions are controlled
remote access sessions are monitored

practices.title: Employ cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants to know which encryption protects each remote access method and whether it is in use. For Microsoft 365 the sessions run over TLS, so they look for legacy protocols and old TLS versions being refused; for VPN or remote desktop they read the configuration for the protocol and ciphers. They ask whether the cryptography uses FIPS-validated modules. Testing means connecting with an old protocol and seeing it refused.
common_failure_modes: The encryption for VPN or remote desktop is not documented at all.
Legacy TLS clients or basic SMTP authentication are still allowed.
No one can say whether the VPN uses FIPS-validated cryptography.
A vendor remote support tool is used with no record of how its sessions are protected.

objectives.determination: cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions are identified
cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions are implemented

practices.title: Route remote access via managed access control points.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that remote access enters through a small number of managed points, such as Entra sign-in with Conditional Access, a VPN gateway or a remote desktop gateway, and not straight to individual systems. They read the list of those points and the rules on each, then look for paths around them, like a server with remote desktop open to the internet. In the tenant they read the Conditional Access policy that blocks access from anywhere except approved locations or paths.
common_failure_modes: The managed access points are not listed.
A server or device accepts remote desktop or SSH straight from the internet.
No Conditional Access policy blocks access from outside the approved locations.
Users can sign in to CUI resources from anywhere because location exclusions are too broad.

objectives.determination: managed access control points are identified and implemented
remote access is routed through managed network access control points

practices.title: Authorize remote execution of privileged commands and remote access to security-relevant information.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants a list of privileged commands that may be run remotely and of security information that may be viewed remotely (for example audit logs, security alerts, configuration), and who is authorized for each. They then check that remote privileged access requires a strong sign-in and that roles are activated through PIM with a reason. They sample a few remote privileged sessions or activations and match them to an authorized person.
common_failure_modes: Remote privileged access is allowed but never listed or authorized in writing.
Admin roles can be used remotely without MFA or a phishing-resistant method.
Security logs and alerts can be read by people with no recorded need.
Role activations carry no reason, so their authorization cannot be checked.

objectives.determination: privileged commands authorized for remote execution are identified
security-relevant information authorized to be accessed remotely is identified
the execution of the identified privileged commands via remote access is authorized
access to the identified security-relevant information via remote access is authorized

practices.title: Authorize wireless access prior to allowing such connections.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks for a list of the organization's wireless access points and how a device is allowed to join them. They read the wireless configuration, looking for enterprise authentication (each device or user authenticates) rather than a shared password, and the Intune Wi-Fi profiles pushed to managed devices. Testing means trying to join from an unapproved device and seeing it refused.
common_failure_modes: There is no list of access points, or a guest network is left off it.
Wireless uses a shared password known to staff and visitors alike.
Rogue or forgotten access points are found during a walk-through.
The organization says it has no wireless but staff connect to an office network anyway.

objectives.determination: wireless access points are identified
wireless access is authorized prior to allowing such connections

practices.title: Protect wireless access using authentication and encryption.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that wireless networks need authentication and encrypt traffic, normally WPA2 or WPA3, ideally enterprise mode. They read the access point configuration and the Intune Wi-Fi profiles and compare them. Guest networks must not reach CUI. Testing means looking at the network's security settings from a client and confirming an open network is not available.
common_failure_modes: An open or WEP network is still broadcast.
The guest network can reach internal systems.
Access point settings and the Intune profiles disagree.

objectives.determination: wireless access to the system is protected using authentication
wireless access to the system is protected using encryption

practices.title: Control connection of mobile devices.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants a list of mobile devices that touch CUI and the rule for letting them connect. They compare the list with the phones and tablets enrolled in Intune, read the Conditional Access policy that only lets compliant devices or approved apps reach CUI, and check that connections are logged. Testing means trying to reach CUI from an unenrolled phone and seeing it blocked.
common_failure_modes: No list of mobile devices that handle CUI.
Personal phones reach CUI mail through the native mail app without any device or app control.
The Conditional Access policy leaves out iOS or Android.
Mobile sign-ins are not logged or not reviewed.

objectives.determination: mobile devices that process, store, or transmit CUI are identified
mobile device connections are authorized
mobile device connections are monitored and logged

practices.title: Encrypt CUI on mobile devices and mobile computing platforms.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks which mobile devices and platforms hold CUI and that CUI on them is encrypted. For managed phones that is device encryption enforced by compliance policy; for personal phones it is app protection that encrypts app data. They read the Intune app protection and compliance policies and compare them with the device list. They look at a sample device's compliance state.
common_failure_modes: The list of mobile platforms with CUI is missing or leaves out laptops used on the road.
App protection does not encrypt app data, or covers iOS but not Android.
Compliance policy does not require device encryption.

objectives.determination: mobile devices and mobile computing platforms that process, store, or transmit CUI are identified
encryption is employed to protect CUI on identified mobile devices and mobile computing platforms

practices.title: Verify and control/limit connections to and use of external information systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants to know which external systems connect to or are used with the organization's system: partner tenants, personal devices, cloud services, file-sharing sites. They check each is listed, that its security has been checked (for example by agreement or the provider's attestation), and that the tenant limits it: cross-tenant access defaults, guest and external sharing settings, public Teams, and app protection on personal devices. They sample external sharing and ask why it was allowed.
common_failure_modes: No list of external systems, or personal devices and outside file-sharing services are left out.
The default cross-tenant setting allows all external users in.
SharePoint or Teams allows anonymous links or public teams.
Personal phones reach company data without app protection.
Nobody can show how an external system was checked before it was used.

objectives.determination: connections to external systems are identified
the use of external systems is identified
connections to external systems are verified
the use of external systems is verified
connections to external systems are controlled/limited
the use of external systems is controlled/limited

practices.title: Limit use of portable storage devices on external systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks the organization has written down whether CUI may be carried on USB drives or other portable storage to outside systems, and the limits if so (for example only encrypted company drives, only with approval). They read the Intune setting that blocks or limits removable storage on managed devices and compare it with the rule. Testing means plugging a drive into a managed device and seeing what happens.
common_failure_modes: The policy is silent on portable storage used with outside systems.
Removable storage is allowed on all managed devices.
Exceptions are granted informally with no record.

objectives.determination: the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems is identified and documented
limits on the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems are defined
the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems is limited as defined

practices.title:
Control information posted or processed on publicly accessible
information systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks which public systems the organization posts to (website, social media, public file links) and who may post. They want a written review step before anything is posted, a record of reviews, and a way to take down CUI if it slips out. In the tenant they check that SharePoint and OneDrive do not allow anonymous 'Anyone' links and look for anonymous link events in the audit log. They sample recent public posts and ask who reviewed them.
common_failure_modes: No list of who may post to the website or social media.
Posts go out with no recorded review.
SharePoint allows anonymous 'Anyone' links, or the audit log shows them being created.
Nobody knows how to take down content if CUI is posted by mistake.

objectives.determination: individuals authorized to post or process information on publicly accessible systems are identified
procedures to ensure CUI is not posted or processed on publicly accessible systems are identified
a review process is in place prior to posting of any content to publicly accessible systems
content on publicly accessible systems is reviewed to ensure that it does not include CUI
mechanisms are in place to remove and address improper posting of CUI

practices.title: Ensure that managers, system administrators and users of organizational systems are made aware of the security risks associated with their activities and of the applicable policies, standards and procedures related to the security of those systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the awareness program description and the course material to confirm two things: it explains the risks that come with the organization's own work on CUI, and it points people to the security policies and procedures that apply to them. They then pick a sample of managers, administrators and ordinary users from the current account list and look for a completion record for each one inside the refresh cycle the policy states. In interviews they ask those people to name a risk from their own job and say where the security policies are kept. Testing means showing that the tracking method flags people who are overdue and picks up new accounts.
common_failure_modes: An off-the-shelf course that never mentions CUI or the organization's own policies.
Completion records exist for only part of the workforce; administrators, contractors or part-time staff are missing.
No refresh cycle is written down, or the latest completions are older than the cycle the policy claims.
The risks were never identified in writing, so the course content is the only place they appear.
Interviewed staff cannot say where the security policies live or which ones apply to them.

objectives.determination: security risks associated with organizational activities involving CUI are identified
policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of the system are identified
managers, systems administrators, and users of the system are made aware of the security risks associated with their activities
managers, systems administrators, and users of the system are made aware of the applicable policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of the system

practices.title: Ensure that personnel are trained to carry out their assigned information security- related duties and responsibilities.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a written list of security duties by role (for example who manages accounts, who reviews logs, who handles incidents, who approves changes) and checks that every role has a named person today. For each named person they want a training record that fits the role, not only the general awareness course everyone takes. They interview a few role holders about what their security duties are and what training prepared them, and compare the people holding privileged rights in the tenant against the role list. There is no automated signal for this practice in CES; it rests on documents, training records and interviews.
common_failure_modes: Roles are described but nobody is named, or the names are stale after staff changes.
Role holders have only the general awareness course and nothing tied to their duties.
People with administrator rights in the tenant do not appear in the role list at all.
The policy does not say which training each role needs, so adequacy cannot be judged.
Role holders describe duties in interview that differ from what the documents say.

objectives.determination: information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities are defined
information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities are assigned to designated personnel
personnel are adequately trained to carry out their assigned information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities

practices.title: Provide security awareness training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that the organization has written down what warning signs of an insider threat look like in its setting (for example unusual data movement, attempts to get around controls, unexplained access requests) and that training teaches managers and employees to spot those signs and how to report them. They examine the course material and completion records for a sample of managers and staff, and in interviews ask people what they would do and whom they would tell if they saw a warning sign. Testing means confirming the reporting channel named in the training actually exists and reaches someone.
common_failure_modes: Insider threat appears as a single slide in the general course with no list of warning signs.
The training never says how or to whom a concern should be reported, or names a person who has left.
Managers receive no coverage of their part in spotting and escalating warning signs.
Completion records for the insider threat course are missing for part of the workforce.

objectives.determination: potential indicators associated with insider threats are identified
security awareness training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat is provided to managers and employees

practices.title: Create and retain system audit logs and records to the extent needed to enable the monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the audit and accountability policy for two written decisions: which event types must be logged and what each record must contain, and how long records are kept. They then compare those decisions with what the tenant and the Azure resources actually log. They pull a sample of recent records from the unified audit log and the Log Analytics workspace and check that each one carries the defined fields, such as event, time, actor, source and outcome. They check the retention settings in Purview and Log Analytics against the written period and ask for an old record from near the end of that period. In interviews they ask the logging administrator how the event list was chosen and how a gap in logging would be noticed.
common_failure_modes: The policy says logging is enabled but never lists the event types or the record content it needs.
Unified audit logging is off, or some workloads in scope (Exchange, SharePoint, Entra ID, Azure resources) send nothing.
Azure resources holding CUI have no diagnostic settings, so their activity never reaches the workspace.
The written retention period differs from the Purview or Log Analytics setting, or no period is written at all.
No record older than a few weeks can be produced, so retention cannot be shown in practice.
Sampled records lack a field the policy says they must carry.

objectives.determination: audit logs needed (i.e., event types to be logged) to enable the monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system
the content of audit records needed to support monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity is defined
audit records are created (generated)
audit records, once created, contain the defined content
retention requirements for audit records are defined
audit records are retained as defined

practices.title: Ensure that the actions of individual system users can be uniquely traced to those users so they can be held accountable for their actions.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that the organization has written down which record fields tie an action to one person, normally the user principal name or object id, plus time and source. They pick a few recent actions, such as a sign-in, a role change and a file access, and follow each record back to a single named account. They look at whether shared or generic accounts exist and, if they do, how actions on them are tied to a person. In interviews they ask how the organization would show who made a given change last week. CES reads the Entra sign-in and directory audit logs and checks that every record names an actor.
common_failure_modes: Shared admin or service accounts are used for interactive work, so actions cannot be tied to one person.
Records name only an application or an IP address for actions a person took.
The policy never says which fields identify the user, so the defined content cannot be checked.
Logs from some systems use local accounts that cannot be matched to directory identities.

objectives.determination: the content of the audit records needed to support the ability to uniquely trace users to their actions is defined
audit records, once created, contain the defined content

practices.title: Review and update logged events.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a written process that says when the list of logged event types is reviewed, for example yearly and after an incident or a major change, and who does it. They ask for the record of the last review and then for what changed as a result: event types or analytics rules added, removed or tuned. They compare the dated review record with the change history of the logging configuration. CES reads Sentinel and Defender alerts for this practice, but alerts alone do not show a review; the review record has to be examined.
common_failure_modes: No review frequency or trigger is written down.
A review is claimed but no dated record of it exists.
The review found gaps but the logging configuration or analytics rules never changed.
The event list has not changed since the system was first set up.

objectives.determination: a process for determining when to review logged events is defined
event types being logged are reviewed in accordance with the defined review process
event types being logged are updated based on the review

practices.title: Alert in the event of an audit logging process failure.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that the organization has written down which logging failures raise an alert, for example a connector that stops sending, an ingestion gap, or storage reaching its limit, and who receives the alert. They examine the alert rule and the action group it notifies and confirm the recipients are current people or a monitored mailbox. Testing means seeing an alert actually reach someone, either from a past failure or a controlled test. CES reads security alerts here, but alerts existing do not show a logging-failure rule; the rule and its recipients have to be examined.
common_failure_modes: No alert exists for a logging failure; problems are found only when someone goes looking.
The action group sends to a former employee or an unmonitored mailbox.
The policy does not say which failures count, so the alert rules cannot be judged against it.
Alerts fire but nobody can show one was received or acted on.

objectives.determination: personnel or roles to be alerted in the event of an audit logging process failure are identified
types of audit logging process failures for which alert will be generated are defined
identified personnel or roles are alerted in the event of an audit logging process failure

practices.title: Correlate audit record review, analysis and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious or unusual activity.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the procedure for reviewing and analyzing audit records and reporting what is found, and checks that it ties these steps together across sources rather than reviewing each log on its own. They look at how sign-in, email, endpoint and cloud records come together, normally in Sentinel or Defender incidents that group alerts from several sources. They sample recent incidents and ask the analyst how one was investigated and reported. CES reads security incidents and checks for recent ones that combine alerts from two or more detection sources.
common_failure_modes: Each system's log is reviewed separately and nothing links them.
The procedure describes review but not how findings are reported or handed to incident response.
No incidents in recent months combine alerts from more than one source.
Analysts cannot show how a sampled incident was investigated or closed.

objectives.determination: audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious, or unusual activity are defined
defined audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes are correlated

practices.title: Provide audit record reduction and report generation to support on-demand analysis and reporting.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks the administrator to run a filtered search on demand, for example all actions by one user over a date range, and then produce a report from the result. They watch it done, check that the filter actually reduces the records to what was asked, and that the report can be saved or shared. They examine any saved queries or workbooks used for routine reporting. CES runs a date-bounded unified audit log search and keeps the result for on-demand analysis.
common_failure_modes: Searching means scrolling raw logs; no filter or query capability is in use.
Only one person knows how to run a search, and they are not available.
Reports cannot be produced without exporting raw data and working on it by hand.
The search tool cannot reach the full retention period.

objectives.determination: an audit record reduction capability that supports on-demand analysis is provided
a report generation capability that supports on-demand reporting is provided

practices.title: Provide a system capability that compares and synchronizes internal system clocks with an authoritative source to generate time stamps for audit records.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that audit records take their time stamps from system clocks, that an authoritative time source is named, and that devices are set to synchronize with it. Microsoft runs time synchronization for its cloud services, so the assessor focuses on endpoints and servers in scope. They examine the Intune policy that configures the Windows time client, confirm it names the authoritative source and is assigned to the in-scope devices, and on a sample device compare its clock and time configuration with the source. CES reads the Intune configuration and checks for an assigned policy that sets the NTP server.
common_failure_modes: No authoritative time source is written down.
The time policy exists but is not assigned to any group, so it applies to no device.
Devices point to a time server different from the one the policy names.
Servers or network devices outside Intune keep their own clocks with no synchronization.

objectives.determination: internal system clocks are used to generate time stamps for audit records
an authoritative source with which to compare and synchronize internal system clocks is specified
internal system clocks used to generate time stamps for audit records are compared to and synchronized with the specified authoritative time source

practices.title: Protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks who can read, change or delete audit records and the tools that manage them, and how that is enforced. They examine role assignments for audit and compliance roles in Entra and Purview, RBAC on the Log Analytics workspace and log storage account, resource locks, and any immutable (WORM) storage for logs. They ask a user without those roles to try to open the audit log, and they check that deleting or editing a record is blocked or itself logged. No tenant signal in CES covers this practice; it rests on role and configuration records, AdminOps checks and tests.
common_failure_modes: Many accounts hold Compliance Administrator or workspace Contributor rights with no stated need.
Log storage has no immutability or delete lock, so an administrator could erase records.
Protection covers the logs but not the tools, such as Sentinel rules, diagnostic settings or retention policies.
Retention policies can be shortened by the same people whose actions are being logged.
Nobody can show what happens when someone tries to delete audit data.

objectives.determination: audit information is protected from unauthorized access
audit information is protected from unauthorized modification
audit information is protected from unauthorized deletion
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized access
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized modification
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized deletion

practices.title: Limit management of audit logging functionality to a subset of privileged users.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a written list of the privileged users allowed to manage audit logging, a smaller group than all administrators. They compare that list with who actually holds the roles that can change audit settings: Compliance Administrator and audit roles in Purview, Sentinel Contributor, and owner or contributor rights on the logging resources. They check that general IT administrators who are not on the list cannot change audit settings, and ask how the list is approved and reviewed. No tenant signal in CES covers this practice; the evidence is the role assignment records and interviews.
common_failure_modes: No written subset exists; every Global Administrator can manage logging.
The list names people, but the tenant grants audit management roles to others as well.
Subscription owners can change diagnostic settings even though they are not on the list.
The list is never reviewed after staff or role changes.

objectives.determination: a subset of privileged users granted access to manage audit logging functionality is defined
management of audit logging functionality is limited to the defined subset of privileged users

practices.title: Establish and maintain baseline configurations and inventories of organizational systems (including hardware, software, firmware, and documentation) throughout the respective system development life cycles.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks for the documented baseline for each kind of system in scope (workstations, servers, cloud tenant, network gear) and checks that it covers hardware, software, firmware and the documents that describe the system. They then ask for the system inventory and compare it, line by line for a sample, against what the management tools actually see, such as the devices enrolled in Intune. Interviews cover who owns the baseline and the inventory, how often each is reviewed, and what happens when a device is bought, rebuilt or retired. Testing means picking a few real devices and confirming they appear in the inventory and carry the baseline settings, and picking a few inventory rows and confirming the device still exists.
common_failure_modes: The baseline is a vendor template that was never adapted or approved for this environment.
Firmware and system documentation are left out of both the baseline and the inventory.
The inventory is a spreadsheet that does not match the devices enrolled in the management tool.
There is no record of a review: the baseline and the inventory carry no dates, versions or owners.
Cloud services, virtual machines or network equipment that handle CUI are missing from the inventory.

objectives.determination: a baseline configuration is established
the baseline configuration includes hardware, software, firmware, and documentation
the baseline configuration is maintained (reviewed and updated) throughout the system development life cycle
a system inventory is established
the system inventory includes hardware, software, firmware, and documentation
the inventory is maintained (reviewed and updated) throughout the system development life cycle

practices.title: Establish and enforce security configuration settings for information technology products employed in organizational systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the security configuration settings the organization has chosen for each product in use (for example a CIS benchmark or Microsoft security baseline, with any documented deviations) and checks that those settings are part of the baseline from 3.4.1. They then look for proof the settings are pushed and kept in place, not just written down: deployed configuration profiles, compliance policies and drift reports. Interviews ask who approves a deviation from the chosen settings and how drift is caught. Testing means checking a sample device or the tenant itself for a handful of the documented settings and seeing whether the value matches.
common_failure_modes: Settings are documented for Windows endpoints only; servers, the cloud tenant or network devices have none.
Configuration profiles exist but are assigned to no devices or only to a pilot group.
Deviations from the chosen benchmark are in place on devices but never written down or approved.
Nobody looks at drift or compliance reports, so devices that fell out of compliance stay that way.

objectives.determination: security configuration settings for information technology products employed in the system are established and included in the baseline configuration
security configuration settings for information technology products employed in the system are enforced

practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a change control process that covers the systems in scope and asks to see its records: a ticket or request for each change, a review of it, an approve or reject decision by someone with the authority to make it, and a log entry showing the change was made. They take a sample of real changes from the tenant audit log and trace each one back to an approved request, then take a sample of requests and trace each one forward to the logged change. Interviews ask administrators how they raise a change and what they do in an emergency. Unrecorded changes in the audit log are the usual finding.
common_failure_modes: Changes appear in the tenant audit log with no matching request or approval.
The same administrator requests, approves and makes the change with no second review.
Rejected changes are not recorded, so there is no evidence that disapproval is possible.
Emergency changes are made and never reviewed or recorded afterwards.
The change log covers the ticketing system only and leaves out cloud or firewall changes.

objectives.determination: changes to the system are tracked
changes to the system are reviewed
changes to the system are approved or disapproved
changes to the system are logged

practices.title:
Analyze the security impact of changes prior to implementation.
Assessment Objective:
[a] the security impact of changes to the system is analyzed prior to implementation.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that changes are judged for their security effect before they go in, not after. They read the change procedure for a step that asks what the change does to security controls, and pick a sample of recent changes to see a written security impact analysis on each one, dated before the change was made. Interviews ask who performs the analysis, what they look at (affected controls, new access, new data flows, the SSP) and what happens when an impact is found. Testing means comparing the dates of the analysis with the date the change appears in the audit log.
common_failure_modes: The change form has a security impact field that is always left blank or says "none".
The analysis is written after the change was already made.
The person doing the analysis has no security knowledge and no checklist to follow.
Changes that alter the system boundary or data flows never lead to an update of the SSP.

objectives.determination: the security impact of changes to the system is analyzed prior to implementation

practices.title: Define, document, approve and enforce physical and logical access restrictions associated with changes to organizational systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks two kinds of restriction on who can make changes. For physical changes they look for written rules on who may enter server rooms, network closets or equipment areas to change hardware, and proof those rules are approved and applied (badge lists, key logs, visitor logs). For logical changes they look for a written list of who holds administrative roles in the tenant and on systems, approval of that list, and proof that only those people hold the rights. Interviews ask how a person gets and loses change rights. Testing means comparing the approved list with the people who actually hold privileged roles today.
common_failure_modes: Physical restrictions on changes are not written down; the server closet is open to anyone in the office.
The list of people allowed to make changes was never approved by anyone with authority.
More people hold Global Administrator or other privileged roles than the approved list allows.
Former staff or shared accounts still hold administrative rights.

objectives.determination: physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are defined
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are documented
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are approved
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are enforced
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are defined
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are documented
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are approved
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are enforced

practices.title: Employ the principle of least functionality by configuring organizational systems to provide only essential capabilities.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks the organization to show which capabilities each system needs to do its job, and then checks that the systems are set up to offer only those. They read the documented list of essential functions for each system role and compare it with the configuration profiles actually deployed. Interviews ask administrators how they decided what is essential and who approves turning a capability back on. Testing means checking a sample device for capabilities the list calls nonessential (consumer features, Bluetooth, unused roles) and seeing whether they are turned off.
common_failure_modes: No list of essential capabilities exists, so there is nothing to configure against.
Devices are left at manufacturer or default settings with consumer features turned on.
Restrictions apply to some device groups but not to others that handle CUI.

objectives.determination: essential system capabilities are defined based on the principle of least functionality
the system is configured to provide only the defined essential capabilities

practices.title: Restrict, disable or prevent the use of nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols and services.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor works through five categories: programs, functions, ports, protocols and services. For each one they look for a written statement of what is essential and what is not, and a configuration that restricts, disables or blocks what is not. They read application control settings, firewall rules and service configurations, and ask administrators how each list was built and how exceptions are approved. Testing means checking a sample device or network segment: trying to run a program that should be blocked, scanning for open ports, and confirming that disabled services and protocols are really off.
common_failure_modes: Programs are covered but ports, protocols and services have no defined list.
Firewall rules allow any traffic inbound or outbound with no written reason.
Legacy protocols such as SMBv1, Telnet or basic authentication are still enabled.
Application control runs in audit mode only and blocks nothing.
Exceptions are granted without a record of who approved them and why.

objectives.determination: essential programs are defined
the use of nonessential programs is defined
the use of nonessential programs is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined
essential functions are defined
the use of nonessential functions is defined
the use of nonessential functions is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined
essential ports are defined
the use of nonessential ports is defined
the use of nonessential ports is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined
essential protocols are defined
the use of nonessential protocols is defined
the use of nonessential protocols is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined
essential services are defined
the use of nonessential services is defined
the use of nonessential services is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined

practices.title: Apply deny-by-exception (blacklisting) policy to prevent the use of unauthorized software or deny-all, permit-by-exception (whitelisting) policy to allow the execution of authorized software.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor first reads the policy to see which approach the organization chose: deny by exception (a list of software that is blocked) or permit by exception (only listed software may run). They then read the list itself and check that it is specific and current. Testing is the core of this practice: they compare the software actually found on devices with the list, and on a sample device try to run something that the policy says should not run. Interviews ask who maintains the list and how a new program gets approved.
common_failure_modes: The policy does not say which approach is used, or says one and the devices use the other.
The software list is missing, generic, or years out of date.
Software found on devices includes items the list says are blocked or does not allow.
Application control is configured but not assigned to the devices that handle CUI.

objectives.determination: a policy specifying whether whitelisting or blacklisting is to be implemented is specified
the software allowed to execute under whitelisting or denied use under blacklisting is specified
whitelisting to allow the execution of authorized software or blacklisting to prevent the use of unauthorized software is implemented as specified

practices.title: Control and monitor user-installed software.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the policy on whether users may install software and, if so, what and how. They check that device settings carry out that policy, for example by removing local administrator rights, blocking sideloading or limiting installs to an approved company portal. They then look for monitoring: a report of the software installed on devices that someone reviews and acts on. Interviews ask users how they get a new program and ask administrators how they spot an unapproved install. Testing means trying to install an unapproved program on a sample device as a standard user.
common_failure_modes: Users still have local administrator rights and can install anything.
The policy says installs are controlled but no device setting enforces it.
Installed software reports exist but nobody reviews them or follows up on findings.

objectives.determination: a policy for controlling the installation of software by users is established
installation of software by users is controlled based on the established policy
installation of software by users is monitored

practices.title: Identify information system users, processes acting on behalf of users or devices.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the identification and authentication policy and asks for three lists: people with accounts, non-person identities (service accounts, application registrations, managed identities) and devices that reach the system. They match the account list against the current staff and contractor roster and look for accounts nobody owns or several people use. For non-person identities they want a purpose and a named owner for each. For devices they compare the hardware inventory with the devices registered or enrolled in the tenant. Testing means taking a few recent sign-ins and tracing each one to a single person or identity and a known device.
common_failure_modes: Shared or generic logins (front desk, shop floor, a team mailbox used to sign in) that several people use.
Scripts and integrations run under a person's own account instead of a dedicated identity.
Service accounts and application registrations have no recorded purpose or owner.
Devices that reach CUI are not registered or enrolled, so they cannot be told apart.
Accounts remain for people who no longer appear on the staff or contractor roster.

objectives.determination: system users are identified
processes acting on behalf of users are identified
devices accessing the system are identified

practices.title: Authenticate (or verify) the identities of those users, processes, or devices, as a prerequisite to allowing access to organizational information systems.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that nothing reaches the system without first proving who or what it is. They read the policy and the tenant's authentication methods and sign-in rules for users, look at how service accounts and applications authenticate (secrets, certificates, managed identities), and ask how a device proves itself before it is trusted. They interview the identity administrator about any path that skips authentication, such as anonymous sharing links, kiosk sessions or legacy protocols. Testing means trying to reach a protected resource without signing in, and reading sign-in logs for user, application and device sign-ins.
common_failure_modes: Anonymous or "anyone with the link" sharing gives access to CUI without any sign-in.
Applications and service accounts use shared or hard-coded secrets that several systems know.
Devices are trusted by network location alone, with no device identity check.
Legacy protocols still allow sign-in that bypasses the modern authentication rules.
The policy names the methods but the tenant has a different set enabled.

objectives.determination: the identity of each user is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access
the identity of each process acting on behalf of a user is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access
the identity of each device accessing or connecting to the system is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access

practices.title: Use multi-factor authentication for local and network access to privileged accounts and for network access to non-privileged accounts.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor first asks for the list of privileged accounts and compares it with the people who actually hold administrator roles in the tenant and on local machines. They then read the sign-in rules (Conditional Access) to see that every privileged and every ordinary account must use a second factor for network access, and look at how administrators sign in locally to servers and workstations. They look at who is excluded from the rules and why, and at the per-user registration report for accounts with no second factor registered. Testing means signing in as a sampled privileged and a sampled ordinary user from outside and watching for the second-factor prompt, and checking local administrator sign-in on a sample machine.
common_failure_modes: The privileged account list is missing local administrator accounts or accounts with roles assigned outside the main admin groups.
Conditional Access exclusions go beyond the documented break-glass accounts.
Some enabled accounts have no second factor registered, so the rule cannot apply to them.
Local sign-in to servers or workstations with an administrator account uses a password only.
Multifactor is required only from untrusted locations, so office network access skips it.

objectives.determination: privileged accounts are identified
multifactor authentication is implemented for local access to privileged accounts
multifactor authentication is implemented for network access to privileged accounts
multifactor authentication is implemented for network access to non-privileged accounts

practices.title: Employ replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to privileged and non-privileged accounts.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks which authentication methods protect network sign-in and whether each one resists replay, meaning a captured sign-in cannot be used again (for example one-time codes, challenge-response, FIDO2 keys, certificates, Kerberos). They read the authentication strength definitions and the Conditional Access rules that require them, and check that they cover privileged and ordinary accounts. They interview the identity administrator about protocols that send reusable secrets, such as basic authentication to mail or older VPNs. Testing means confirming in sign-in logs that sampled accounts used a replay-resistant method, and that legacy protocols are refused.
common_failure_modes: A phishing-resistant strength is defined but no enabled policy requires it.
The required strength still allows a weaker method, so users fall back to it.
Older VPN, mail or line-of-business protocols accept a plain password that can be replayed.
Only administrators are covered; ordinary accounts sign in with a reusable password.

objectives.determination: replay-resistant authentication mechanisms are implemented for network account access to privileged and non-privileged accounts

practices.title: Prevent the reuse of identifiers for a defined period.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor looks for a written period during which a retired identifier (a user name or account id) cannot be given to someone else, and for the procedure that enforces it. They compare deleted and disabled accounts with current accounts to see whether any user name was handed to a new person inside the period. They ask the identity administrator what happens when a new hire has the same name as a former employee. Testing means taking a few recently retired identifiers and checking that none is held by a newer account.
common_failure_modes: No reuse period is written down anywhere.
A former employee's user name or mailbox was reassigned to a new hire inside the period.
The naming procedure has no rule for duplicate names, so reuse depends on who creates the account.
Deleted accounts are purged permanently with no record of the identifiers they held.

objectives.determination: a period within which identifiers cannot be reused is defined
reuse of identifiers is prevented within the defined period

practices.title: Disable identifiers after a defined period of inactivity.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the policy for the period of inactivity after which an account is disabled, then compares the last sign-in date of every enabled account with that period. They ask who runs the check, how often, and how service accounts and break-glass accounts are handled. Testing means sorting enabled accounts by last sign-in and confirming none is older than the defined period, or that any exception is documented and approved.
common_failure_modes: The inactivity period is not defined, or differs between the policy and the procedure.
Enabled accounts have not signed in for longer than the defined period.
The check is run by hand, irregularly, with no record of when it last ran.
Service and shared accounts are left out of the check without a documented exception.

objectives.determination: a period of inactivity after which an identifier is disabled is defined
identifiers are disabled after the defined period of inactivity

practices.title: Enforce a minimum password complexity and change of characters when new passwords are created.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the policy for the password rules: minimum length, composition, and how many characters must change when a new password is created. They then look at the settings that enforce those rules in the directory, on devices (compliance and configuration policies) and in any system with its own local passwords. They interview the identity administrator about where passwords still exist and which rules each place enforces. Testing means trying to set a password that breaks the rules and seeing it refused, and reconciling the policy value, the planned parameter and the tenant setting.
common_failure_modes: The policy states a length or composition rule that no system setting enforces.
Device or local-account password settings are weaker than the directory's.
No rule for change of characters is written, or it is written but nothing can enforce it.
Systems with their own local passwords (network gear, line-of-business apps) are not covered.
The values in the policy, the plan and the tenant do not agree.

objectives.determination: password complexity requirements are defined
password change of character requirements are defined
minimum password complexity requirements as defined are enforced when new passwords are created
minimum password change of character requirements as defined are enforced when new passwords are created

practices.title: Prohibit password reuse for a specified number of generations.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the policy for how many previous passwords a user may not reuse, then checks that the setting is enforced wherever passwords are kept: device compliance or configuration policies, local accounts, and any system outside the directory. They interview the administrator about how cloud accounts handle reuse. Testing means changing a test account's password back to a recent one and seeing it refused.
common_failure_modes: The number of generations is not specified, or the policy and settings disagree.
The history setting is enforced on some devices or systems but not others.
Systems with local passwords have no history setting at all.

objectives.determination: the number of generations during which a password cannot be reused is specified
reuse of passwords is prohibited during the specified number of generations

practices.title:
Allow temporary password use for system logons with an immediate change to a permanent password.
Assessment Objective:
[a] an immediate change to a permanent password is required when a temporary password is used for system logon.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor asks how temporary passwords are issued (new accounts, resets, help desk) and checks that each one forces a change to a permanent password at first sign-in. They read the reset procedure and the tenant settings for temporary access codes, and ask the help desk to walk through a reset. Testing means issuing a temporary password to a test account and confirming that the first sign-in demands a new password, and that the temporary one stops working.
common_failure_modes: Temporary passwords issued by the help desk do not force a change at first sign-in.
Temporary access codes can be reused or last longer than the procedure allows.
The same starting password is given to every new account.
Systems outside the directory let users keep the temporary password.

objectives.determination: an immediate change to a permanent password is required when a temporary password is used for system logon

practices.title: Store and transmit only cryptographically protected passwords.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor checks that passwords are never stored or sent in readable form. For storage they ask where passwords and secrets live (the directory, local accounts, application configuration, scripts, password managers) and how each is protected. For transmission they check that sign-in uses encrypted channels and that legacy protocols that send passwords in the clear are blocked. They interview administrators about service account and application secrets. Testing means looking for secrets in scripts or configuration files and confirming legacy authentication is refused.
common_failure_modes: Service account passwords or application secrets are kept in scripts, spreadsheets or plain configuration files.
Legacy authentication is still allowed for some users or protocols.
Network devices or older applications accept passwords over unencrypted channels.
Application secrets never expire and are not rotated.

objectives.determination: passwords are cryptographically protected in storage
passwords are cryptographically protected in transit

practices.title: Obscure feedback of authentication information.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor watches people sign in to the systems in scope and checks that passwords and codes are masked on screen and that error messages do not say which part was wrong. Most of this comes from the platform's sign-in pages, so the assessor also looks at any custom sign-in screen, local console, or line-of-business application the organization runs. CES does not test this in the tenant; it rests on observation and interview.
common_failure_modes: A custom or line-of-business application shows the password as it is typed.
Error messages say whether the user name or the password was wrong.
Shared screens or kiosks show codes or passwords in clear view.

objectives.determination: authentication information is obscured during the authentication process

practices.title: Establish an operational incident-handling capability for organizational systems that includes preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery, and user response activities.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the incident response policy and plan to see that each phase is written down for this organization: how the team gets ready, how incidents are spotted, how they are analysed, how they are contained, how systems are brought back, and what ordinary users must do when something looks wrong. They check that named people hold the incident roles today and have the access and training to act. They then pick recent alerts and incidents from the security console and trace each one through the phases the plan describes, looking for an owner, a status change and a timestamp at each step. In interviews they ask the incident lead to walk through a recent case and ask a few users how they would report a suspected incident. Testing means following one real or exercise incident from detection to closure and confirming that what happened matches the plan.
common_failure_modes: The plan is a template that names no people, tools or contact details for this organization.
Alerts sit in the console as new and unassigned for weeks, so detection exists but nobody analyses what it finds.
Containment steps such as disabling an account or isolating a device are written down, but nobody has the rights or an approval path to carry them out.
Recovery is left to the backup policy with no link to the incident process, so there is no record of how systems were restored and checked.
Users do not know how to report a suspected incident or whom to tell.
The people in incident roles have no training or exercise record tied to that role.

objectives.determination: an operational incident-handling capability is established
the operational incident-handling capability includes preparation
the operational incident-handling capability includes detection
the operational incident-handling capability includes analysis
the operational incident-handling capability includes containment
the operational incident-handling capability includes recovery
the operational incident-handling capability includes user response activities

practices.title: Track, document and report incidents to designated officials and/or authorities both internal and external to the organization.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants one place where incidents are logged, and for every recent incident a record from opening to closure: what happened, when, who handled it, what was done and who was told. They read the reporting section of the plan for the internal officials who must be told (for example the security lead and senior management) and the outside authorities (for a cyber incident affecting CUI under DFARS 252.204-7012, the DoD through the DIBNet portal within 72 hours of discovery), and check that names and contact routes are current. For sampled incidents they look for proof that the right people were notified on time, such as tickets, emails or a DIBNet report number, or a recorded decision that the incident was not reportable. CES has no tenant signal that decides this practice; it rests on records and interviews.
common_failure_modes: Incidents are handled in chat or email with no record that ties the steps together.
Console alerts are closed with no note of what was found or done.
The plan says to report to the appropriate authorities without naming them or saying how to reach them.
No internal official is named, or the named person has left.
A CUI incident has neither a DIBNet report nor a recorded decision that it was not reportable.
Notifications were sent, but nothing shows when, so timeliness cannot be checked.

objectives.determination: incidents are tracked
incidents are documented
authorities to whom incidents are to be reported are identified
organizational officials to whom incidents are to be reported are identified
identified authorities are notified of incidents
identified organizational officials are notified of incidents

practices.title:
Test the organizational incident response capability.
Assessment Objective:
[a] the incident response capability is tested.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the test plan and the record of the most recent exercise: the date, the scenario, who took part, what the exercise was meant to show and what it found. They check that the test happened within the period the policy sets, that it used the organization's own plan, roles and contact lists, and that findings led to changes in the plan or to tracked actions. They interview people who took part about what they did and what changed afterward. Testing means comparing the after-action items with the current plan and the open action list to see that they were acted on. CES has no tenant signal for this practice; it rests on the exercise record and interviews.
common_failure_modes: No exercise has been run, or the last one is older than the cycle the policy states.
The record is only an attendance list, with no scenario, objectives or results.
The exercise used a generic scenario that never touched CUI or the organization's own systems.
Findings from the exercise were never fed back into the plan or tracked to closure.
People who hold key incident roles did not take part.

objectives.determination: the incident response capability is tested

practices.title:
Perform maintenance on organizational systems.
Assessment Objective:
[a] system maintenance is performed.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor reads the maintenance policy and the maintenance schedule to see which systems in the CUI scope get maintained, by whom and how often. They then pick a few recent maintenance events (patch windows, hardware repairs, vendor visits, firmware updates) and ask for the record of each one: date, system, what was done, who did it and who approved it. In interviews they ask the IT lead how maintenance is planned and recorded. Testing means tracing a sampled ticket to the system it names and confirming the work actually shows there. CES has no tenant signal for this practice; it rests on records and interviews.
common_failure_modes: Maintenance happens but nothing records what was done, when or by whom.
The schedule covers servers but leaves out network gear, laptops or cloud-managed systems in scope.
Records exist only for vendor visits; routine in-house work is never written down.
The policy names a maintenance process that staff in interview do not follow.
Sampled tickets cannot be matched to any change on the system they name.

objectives.determination: system maintenance is performed

practices.title: Provide controls on the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used to conduct system maintenance.
practices.what_assessor_does: The assessor wants to see that maintenance is done only with approved tools, by approved methods and by approved people. They read the maintenance policy and look for a list of allowed maintenance tools (remote support software, diagnostic utilities, admin consoles), the approved ways maintenance may be carried out, and a list of people and vendors allowed to do it. They compare the tools installed or used in practice against the list, and the people who did recent maintenance against the authorized list. Interviews cover how a new tool or a new vendor gets approved. CES has no tenant signal for this practice.
